title: Reel 3: Leonard Fields and a great little band heard in 1924
summary: A new reel begins. Waters recalls a small group at a basement club, possibly the original Small's, with saxophonist Leonard Fields, who had the fastest tongue he ever heard.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Still the afternoon of June the 6th, a Sunday in 1982. This is the beginning of our third reel on this particular afternoon, and I am Phil Schaap and this is the interview for the Jazz Oral History Project of Benny Waters, to be archived at the Institute of Jazz Studies, Rutgers University in Newark. Benny, we're gonna break away from the chronology in the second, or actually just leap forward in it to a different period. I want to ask you one last question about the 2 weeks you were in New York in '24. Besides Tricky Sam Nanton, what other people did you hear at that time that impressed you?

Oh, I heard a band with a guy named Leonard Fields, saxophone player and I don't know exactly who was drumming [?] for them. The trumpet player was a guy who used to go around with Sugar Ray Robinson as a valet or something. He played like Louie Armstrong, he sounded like Louie Armstrong and he tried, you see. I can't think of his name now, he was playing just like Louie Armstrong, I mean copy, you know, see. He was really inspired and had that voice all the time, in the street. I just can't pin his name. Well that - and the trombone player, I can't think of either. But that was one of the greatest small combinations that I ever heard. And they were playing now, in that particular music, they had, they were well rehearsed. And this Leonard Fields - I

think he's named Leonard - had the fastest tongue of any negro saxophone player, and I watched it - why I say negro, because when they come down to fast tongues, you go back to the virtuoso, and them virtuosos were white, most of them, you know. 100, 80 per cent, 90 per cent of all of virtuosos on the saxophone were white, you know. And - like Rudy Wiedoft and Benny End [?] and so forth, you now, see. And they - that's their thing, that terrific attack on the, with the tongue, see. And this Leonard Fields, that's what he had, which made his playing distinguished and was one of the fastest saxophone players that I ever heard in my whole life. And that was during the Benny Carter era also, Benny was still 'round, you see, 'cause Benny was born in New York.
You're saying - why did you bring in Benny Carter's name on this?
Well I - because I always admired Benny -
Uh huh. You mean you were saying this guy Leonard Fields played a little like Benny Carter.
No, didn't I, I didn't say, I said he had the fastest tongue of any saxophone player I ever heard, that includes Benny Carter -
That includes Benny Carter, OK. All right, and you heard this Leonard Fields when you were in New York in '24 from Boston, comin' down for two weeks -
At this little jazz club - oh, maybe it was Small's, because Small's had a basement before. Small's had a basement [ ], he had a basement before 7th Avenue, he had a small place there.
So you think it was the original Small's Paradise.

It was. I think, I'm sure it was the original, because it was - I didn't play there. 'Cause it was - I played at the big place. But it was another one there before the big place, I forget, that's where it was. That was the greatest little band I ever heard. They had an arranger - it was no Dixieland band or somethin' like that, it was a band that sounded like they was playin' arrangement but fakin' so well, you know.
